series.title: Reading Solaris
series.deck: A space station where no one comes to meet Kelvin, the Harey who returns, and a hand reaching toward the ocean. Three essays on Stanisław Lem’s novel.
series.source_note: On Stanisław Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris. Essays II and III discuss the ending.

articles.title: No One Came to Meet Him
articles.deck: When Kelvin reaches the station, the first colleague he meets is afraid of him. Recognizing someone may not tell you where they came from.
body: Kelvin’s hatch opened. The station’s machines told him he had docked. When the ventilation cut out, the quiet was uncanny. He had expected someone to meet him. He waited a moment, but there was only a lit arrow pointing to a moving walkway that made no sound. Boxes and gas cylinders cluttered the corridor. Bootprints led away from a patch of oil in several directions.

One door stood ajar. Kelvin recognized the man inside from a photograph. It was Snow. Snow said he didn’t know him. The plastic drinking flask fell from his hand and bounced twice. Kelvin took a step forward, and Snow shrank into his chair. Only when he heard that Kelvin had just flown in from Earth did he say his name.

Kelvin wanted to find Gibarian. He had to ask several times before he learned that Gibarian had died at dawn. Snow didn’t explain how. But as Kelvin was about to leave, Snow stopped him. If he saw anyone other than Snow or Sartorius, he should do nothing at first. Kelvin asked if he meant a hallucination. Snow said it was real. Don’t lay a hand on anyone. Kelvin looked back from the doorway and saw dried blood on the knuckles of both Snow’s hands.

Kelvin knew the station’s layout and could recognize the people who worked there. What baffled him at first was that a colleague could be afraid at the sight of him. Snow had the opposite problem. The man in front of him behaved just like a colleague who had just arrived. After the last few days, though, he could no longer assume that anyone who looked and sounded as expected had come from where he thought they had.

The ocean had posed something like the same problem. Researchers had measured its movements and named the enormous forms that rose from its surface. The names were useful. Without them, two people could hardly tell whether they’d seen the same kind of thing. But recording when a form rises and how it breaks apart only gets you so far toward knowing whether it is answering anyone. Even to say the ocean keeps silent is to sound as though you already know it heard you.

Later, Snow would say that perhaps what people want is a mirror. We go all that way still hoping that somewhere there are eyes like ours that will look back at us. But what Snow asked of Kelvin when he first arrived is harder to do than any of that is to say. Whether the ocean has heard us can be studied for another few decades. When someone actually appears in the corridor, she has already seen you before you can work out where she came from.

articles.title: The Second Harey
articles.deck: The second Harey appears, wearing a shirt as a skirt. This time Kelvin lets her stay, but staying brings its own troubles.
body: Harey asked Kelvin if he was getting in too. He said he’d be right behind her. He had to close the hatch first. She climbed inside. From the hatchway he asked if she had room to sit. When she answered, he pulled back and closed the hatch.

It was a small cargo rocket. The hatch couldn’t be opened from inside. Kelvin had only meant to shut her in for a few hours, long enough to think what to do. Then her blows shook the entire rocket. He rushed to the controls. When the sound from the cabin came through, he made out his own name in a shriek that hardly sounded human. The rocket lifted off. His face was burned. Only after the smoke had thinned could he find the rocket again on the radar.

When Harey appeared again, she called him by the same name. To Kelvin it seemed the same person was standing in front of him once more. But she knew nothing about what had happened in the little rocket. There had been one other witness to that, and Kelvin never heard her voice again. Snow later told him the rocket was still in orbit. They could even try the radio and see if anyone answered. Kelvin refused. The novel doesn’t listen for him, either.

When the first Harey went to change, something took both of them by surprise: the white dress wouldn’t come off. The red buttons were only for show. There wasn’t a fastening anywhere. Kelvin cut a slit in the back so she could pull it over her head. The novel doesn’t show us the ocean making that dress. Still, it’s hard not to think of how memory works. You can remember precisely how someone looked in a dress without ever having seen how she took it off on her own.

The second Harey gradually finds gaps in what she knows. She listens to the recording Gibarian left and goes through what she hears, comparing it with what has happened to her. She asks Kelvin if her blood is the same as his. She asks herself something too: if I’m only pretending to love him, why don’t I know I’m pretending? Kelvin may have known before she did what was strange about her body. This he cannot answer.

Kelvin later tells her that the woman he loves is the one here with him now. Harey knows he’s been good to her. She reminds him that the woman he loved back on Earth wasn’t her. She doesn’t want to hear that story. Kelvin can choose to stay this time. As for whose life this is, Harey has already begun to speak.

articles.title: Between Hand and Sea
articles.deck: Harey leaves a letter, and Kelvin goes down to the ocean. He reaches out to a wave; a thin gap remains between his glove and the water.
body: When Kelvin found Harey in the small workroom, it was so cold inside he could hardly see her. She had swallowed liquid oxygen. He carried her to a table and looked for anything he could use. His hands were too cold even to hold the instruments steady. Before he could think what to do, she opened her eyes. Little by little her body recovered on its own. Later Kelvin told her it was much harder for her to die than for him. To her, that was only frightening.

Kelvin wanted to take her back to Earth. It was the one way forward he could imagine in which they’d both be alive. Snow asked what would happen if the force sustaining her body came from the ocean and she went far from it. Kelvin had no answer. He meant it when he said he wanted to take her with him. But the sincerity of that wish couldn’t tell her whether she would live to see the other end of the trip.

In the end Harey asked Snow for help without telling Kelvin. When Kelvin woke, Snow handed him a letter. Harey had written that she was the one who’d asked. She’d written her name and crossed it out. Snow said Sartorius had built another device. He spoke only of a flash and then a faint movement of air. Kelvin said, “You killed her.” Snow admitted it and asked what Kelvin would have done in his place.

The letter keeps us from treating Harey’s disappearance entirely as something three men decided for her. But being able to ask someone to help her disappear is a long way from being able to leave on her own and live somewhere else. Kelvin wanted her to stay. Snow agreed to help her. Both may have had reasons of their own. When I come to the place where she crossed out her name, I find myself wondering whether, before she had to write that letter, there was anyone there who could have sat with her and helped her think of another way.

The novel doesn’t end with the letter. Later Kelvin lands on an old mimoid on the surface of the ocean and stretches a gloved hand toward the waves. A strand of something gelatinous curls around his fingers and grows upward as he raises his hand. A thin layer of air remains between it and the glove the whole time. Only when Kelvin steps back does it drop back into the waves. He tries more than once. Then a wave recedes as usual, and nothing follows his hand.

Researchers recorded the phenomenon nearly a hundred years earlier. Kelvin has known the description for a long time. When he crouches by the waves himself, that gap is still there. The ocean doesn’t tell him why Harey came. It doesn’t give her back. He is still waiting for something, though he can’t say what.
